items.text: 7 IONIC BONDING

items.label: text
items.text: We have already looked at the definition of a compound. A compound is formed when two or more elements chemically ceo     y a             s  of electrons to form ionic compounds.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 7.1 The properties of a compound are very different from those of the elements. Sodium (an element) is a dangerously reactive metal. It is stored under oil to prevent it reacting with air or water. Chiorine (an element) is a very poisonous, reactive gas. But salt, sodium chloride (an ionic compound), is safe to eat in small quantities.

items.label: section_header
items.text: LEARNING OBJECTIVES

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand how ions are formed by electron loss or gain

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know the charges of these ions:

items.label: list_item
items.text: metals in Groups 1, 2 and 3

items.label: list_item
items.text: non-metals in Groups 5, 6 and 7

items.label: list_item
items.text: Ag⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe²⁺, Fe³⁺, Pb²+, Zn²+

items.label: list_item
items.text: hydrogen (H⁺), hydroxide (OH-), ammonium (NH4+⁺), carbonate (CO_32-), nitrate (NO3-), sulfate (SO4²2-)

items.label: list_item
items.text: Write formulae for compounds formed between the ions listed above

items.label: section_header
items.text: IONIC BONDING

items.label: text
items.text: Sodium chloride is probably the best-known example of an ionic compound -n t    ni o       nic compounds, such as magnesium oxide, calcium fluoride and zinc bromide. What you will realise about all these compounds is that they all contain a metal combined with a non-metal.

items.label: text
items.text: You can recognise ionic compounds because they (usually) contain a metal.

items.label: section_header
items.text: HINT

items.label: text
items.text: There are one or two exceptions to this: there are ionic compounds that do not contain a metal, for example those containing the ammonium ion (such as NH4Cl, (NH4)2SO4. We will look at these later.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Draw dot-and-cross diagrams to show the formation of ionic compounds by electron transfer, limited to combinations of elements from Groups 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7 (only outer electrons need be shown)

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand ionic bonding in terms of electrostatic attractions

items.label: list_item
items.text: Understand why compounds with giant ionic lattices have high melting and boiling points

items.label: list_item
items.text: Know that ionic compounds do not conduct electricity when solid, but do conduct electricity when molten and in aqueous solution
